editorNote: Five unusually distinctive games arrive under a new label while Hollywood turns a modem and a home computer into summer suspense.
morningLine: Games get album covers, computers get briefcases, and WarGames puts dialing into the movies.

lead.headline: Electronic Arts' First Five Games Reach Players
lead.dek: A young publisher treats programmers like recording artists—and ships a remarkably varied opening slate.
body: SOUTH SAN FRANCISCO — Ten days before this week began, the small company called Electronic Arts made its first shipment. Its May 20 slate carried five titles—Archon: The Light and the Dark, Hard Hat Mack, M.U.L.E., Worms?, and Axis Assassin—out of a warehouse and toward computer stores. The boxes announced the company’s ambition before a disk was loaded: creators’ names appeared prominently, and the packages borrowed the scale and visual confidence of record albums.

The selection makes a case for the computer as a broad game machine rather than a single-purpose arcade substitute. M.U.L.E. turns settlement-building into a competitive economy in which supply, demand, land, and luck keep changing the table. Archon begins with the outline of a chessboard, then lets opposing pieces fight their own action contests. Hard Hat Mack brings construction-site timing and hazards to the Apple II, while Axis Assassin and Worms? push in still other directions.

Electronic Arts is selling an identity as much as a catalog. By placing designers in the foreground, the publisher asks buyers to recognize the people behind the software in the way music listeners recognize performers. That approach also gives the first five games a family resemblance without forcing them into one genre.

The first shipping day was hardly glamorous. Company recollections describe the whole crew loading boxes for hours; Nancy Fong remembered, “We all worked all day long,” while Bing Gordon joked that they were terrible warehouse workers. Yet the improvised labor sent out a lineup whose variety and presentation suggest where packaged computer entertainment may be headed.
lead.confidence: Same-month; EA records date the first shipment to May 20, 1983.

stories.headline: WarGames Makes Home Computing a Summer-Movie Star
stories.dek: A teenager, a modem, and a military computer carry a new kind of thriller.
body: WarGames opens June 3 with a home computer and telephone modem at the center of its suspense. Its teenage protagonist reaches a military system while looking for games, then discovers that simulated nuclear conflict can be mistaken for the real thing.

The picture earns $6,227,804 from 843 theaters on its opening weekend, ranking third behind Return of the Jedi and Psycho II. Whatever audiences make of its technical details, the film gives dialing, passwords, artificial intelligence, and computer security a place in the summer-movie vocabulary.
stories.confidence: Exact-date opening and weekend grosses verified.

stories.headline: Portable and 16-Bit Machines Crowd the June BYTE
stories.dek: Greater memory, new processors, and battery power widen the definition of a microcomputer.
body: BYTE’s June cover package surveys 16-bit designs promising more memory and stronger management of it. The featured field ranges from Digital’s Professional 325 and 350 to HP’s Series 200 Model 16, the Intel 80186-based Pronto Series 16, and Olivetti’s Z8000-based M20.

Portability is becoming a serious design claim. The battery-powered Gavilan Mobile Computer can be paired with an optional printer small enough to share a standard briefcase. The same issue also examines the NEC PC-8201, Tim Paterson’s account of MS-DOS, VisiCorp’s Visi On environment, and Digital Research’s DR Logo.

stories.headline: Modems Bring Computer Gamers Together
stories.dek: Telephone lines and organized leagues hint at a social future for home games.
body: Computer Gaming World’s May–June issue places modem gaming and a computer baseball league on its cover, treating remote play as a culture worth watching rather than a laboratory curiosity. Players are beginning to imagine opponents and teammates beyond the room containing the machine.

The $2.75 issue also reviews Computer Ambush, Close Assault, and Germany 1985 and advertises SSI’s Knights of the Desert. Strategy remains central, but the telephone line adds a new possibility: a game community assembled through computers before consumer online services become ordinary.
